screens.title: Interacting with Accounts and Wallets
screens.subtitle: How Ethereum keys, Web3.js accounts, and browser wallets fit together securely

narration.text: In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of Ethereum accounts and the practical ways your dApp should interact with them. An Ethereum account maps a private key — a secret number — to a public address you share. That private key is the gatekeeper to funds and operations, so we must treat it as highly sensitive. For local development, Web3. js can create and import accounts so you can test signing and transactions safely on a local node. But for production users, you should never handle private keys inside the browser. Instead, integrate with wallet software like MetaMask that injects a secure bridge through window. ethereum and performs signing on the user's device. You'll also learn the common pitfalls: storing keys in client code, confusing node-managed accounts with wallet accounts, and failing to handle user denial flows. By the end of this chapter you will be able to create test accounts, sign messages for identity proofs, recover signer addresses, and wire a React dApp to request accounts from MetaMask while following secure patterns. Think about one safety rule as you begin: never ship a private key inside client-side code. How would you design a dApp that never touches a user's private key?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Private keys control access; use Web3.js for local testing, and rely on browser wallets like MetaMask for user-facing signing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Interacting with Accounts and Wallets
Accounts, Keys, and Wallets
A concise orientation for developers: what to generate, what to trust, and what to delegate.
Why this chapter matters

Understanding key ownership and proper signing flows prevents catastrophic losses and keeps users' private keys safe. This chapter pairs practical Web3.js examples for local testing with production-safe integration patterns using browser wallets.

In this lesson
Create test accounts, sign and recover messages, and integrate MetaMask safely.
Keys & Accounts
Public address vs private key and the ownership model for Ethereum.
Local Testing
Use web3.eth.accounts.create and privateKeyToAccount for test flows on Ganache.
Wallet Integration
Use window.ethereum and eth_requestAccounts to ask for user addresses and signing.
Visual Concept
PK
Private Key (secret)
0x..
Public Address (shareable)
Keep private keys off client code. Use wallets to sign and return only signatures.
Quick Safety Tip
Never commit private keys. For production rely on MetaMask or hardware wallets so keys never leave the user's device.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives will guide your learning and the hands-on work you do with accounts and wallets. First, you'll understand the cryptographic model behind Ethereum accounts: how a private key deterministically produces a public address, and why that mapping matters for ownership and recovery. I'll give you an example so you can see how a generated private key yields a unique address. Second, you'll be able to create and manage local accounts using Web3. js for development and testing. That means generating accounts programmatically and importing private keys into a local wallet for scripted tests. Third, you'll know how signing works: how to sign messages or transactions with a private key and then recover the signer's address to prove ownership. You'll practice signing and using the recover method. Finally, you'll be able to integrate a browser wallet like MetaMask into a React dApp, request accounts securely with eth_requestAccounts, and handle user approval or rejection. For each objective I'll also show common mistakes to avoid and concrete checks you can run. These skills together will let you test confidently locally while keeping real user keys safe in production.

First, learn: you will be able to explain how a public address is derived from a private key and why that derivation prevents address collisions. A quick check is to generate two accounts and confirm both addresses differ. Next, understand: you can demonstrate signing by creating a signature for a short message and recovering the signer. The practical check is recovering the address and matching it to the signing account. Then apply: import a Ganache private key into web3. eth. accounts. wallet and send a signed transaction on a local node to observe gas and nonce behavior. Finally, master: implement MetaMask connection code that gracefully handles user rejection and displays a connected address. For each objective we pair a simple test so you know when you have achieved competency. Why this matters

screens.title: What is an Ethereum Account?
screens.subtitle: Public address, private key, and why the mapping matters

narration.text: An Ethereum account is a cryptographic identity: a private key and the public address derived from it. The private key is a randomly generated secret number. The public address is derived in a deterministic way from that private key and begins with 0x. That address is what you share to receive tokens or interact with smart contracts. The private key grants full control: signing a transaction with a private key moves funds or calls contract methods as the account owner. In practice that means protecting the private key is the primary security responsibility. For example, when a developer uses web3. eth. accounts. create during testing, they see a new private key and its corresponding address. If the same private key appears again, the derived address will be identical; otherwise every run generates a new unique pair. A common misconception is to treat addresses as passwords; addresses are public identifiers, not secret protectors. The secret is the private key and it must never be exposed in production client code. Key takeaway: ownership equals possession of the private key, and the address is only the public pointer. How will you ensure private keys never leave secure storage in your next app?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An account = private key (secret) + public address (shareable). Private key controls assets; never expose it.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is an Ethereum Account?
Account components
Private key

A secret number granting full control over the account. Keep it private; losing it loses access. Sharing it grants control to others.

Public address

Derived from the private key and safe to share. It is the identifier you publish to receive tokens.

Concrete example
// Example concept: new random private key produces new address // web3.eth.accounts.create() will return an object with address and privateKey { address: '0x0123...abcd', privateKey: '0xabc123...'} // Key point: change the private key and the address changes deterministically
Misconception check
  • Address is not a secret; it cannot prevent access — only the private key can.
  • Do not store private keys in client-side storage or version control.
Key Takeaway

Private key equals control. Treat it like cash in a locked safe: accessible only by the owner and never baked into public code.

screens.title: Create and Manage Local Accounts with Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Generating accounts, importing private keys, and adding to web3 wallet for testing

narration.text: When developing locally you often need throwaway accounts to run tests and simulate users. Web3. js provides a compact A P I for this. The usual process has four steps: generate a new account, inspect the returned address and private key, import an existing private key into the Web3. js wallet for scripted signing, and list node-managed accounts from the connected provider like Ganache. For example, calling web3. eth. accounts. create() returns an object with address and privateKey; this is convenient for quick tests. If you need to reuse a known private key, privateKeyToAccount transforms that key into an account object you can add to web3. eth. accounts. wallet. Important safety note: never do this with a real private key in client-side production code. Add imported testing keys only in a local Node. js environment or test runner. Also remember Ganache's accounts are available via web3. eth. getAccounts because they are node-managed; those differ from user wallets injected via window. ethereum. A common error is forgetting the 0x prefix on imported keys; privateKeyToAccount expects it. Try generating two accounts and confirm different addresses to validate randomness. At the end, consider how you will separate test-only keys from real user flows.

keyIdea.title: Local account flow
keyIdea.text: Use web3.eth.accounts.create for test keys, privateKeyToAccount plus wallet.add for imports, and web3.eth.getAccounts to inspect node accounts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Create & Manage Local Accounts
Typical steps
  1. Generate a new account with web3.eth.accounts.create(). Record its privateKey only in secure local logs.
  2. To reuse a key, call web3.eth.accounts.privateKeyToAccount(privateKey) and then web3.eth.accounts.wallet.add(account).
  3. Fetch node accounts with web3.eth.getAccounts() to inspect Ganache-provided test accounts.
  4. Never add production private keys to client-side wallet instances; do imports only in Node.js test contexts.
Example Node snippet
const newAccount = web3.eth.accounts.create();
console.log(newAccount.address);
console.log(newAccount.privateKey);

const account = web3.eth.accounts.privateKeyToAccount('0xabcdef...');
web3.eth.accounts.wallet.add(account);
const nodeAccounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
console.log(nodeAccounts);
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting the 0x prefix on private keys when importing.
  • Using test keys in production or committing keys to version control.
  • Confusing node-managed accounts with injected wallet accounts for user interactions.
Key Takeaway

Local account creation is for testing. Keep test keys isolated and never expose real private keys in client code.

screens.title: Signing and Recovering Messages with Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Proof of ownership without revealing private keys

narration.text: Signing proves ownership without exposing the private key. In Web3. js you can sign a message with web3. eth. accounts. sign(message, privateKey), which returns a signature object. That signature can be verified with web3. eth. accounts. recover(message, signature) to yield the signer address. Practically this allows simple authentication flows: your user signs a nonce or challenge and you verify the signer address matches the claimed account. In a local test, you might create a new account, sign the string 'Hello Cohortia...' and then recover the address to confirm the process. Be careful: signing with a raw private key in a browser is unsafe; use this pattern only in server-side or local Node. js tests. Another common point of confusion is message vs transaction signing: message signing signs an arbitrary string and is useful for identity proofs, while transaction signing constructs and signs a full Ethereum transaction object including gas and nonce. Here's a compact code example showing sign and recover for a message. Try it locally and then think about how this pattern maps to server-side login flows where you issue nonces to prevent replay attacks.

keyIdea.title: Signing pattern
keyIdea.text: Sign messages locally with web3.eth.accounts.sign and verify with web3.eth.accounts.recover to prove ownership without sharing private keys.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Signing & Recovering
Sign and verify
const message = 'Hello Cohortia, this is a signed message.';
const signature = web3.eth.accounts.sign(message, newAccount.privateKey);
console.log('Signature:', signature.signature);

const recovered = web3.eth.accounts.recover(message, signature.signature);
console.log('Recovered Address:', recovered);
// Recovered should match newAccount.address
Practical note

Use signed messages for login challenges, signed approvals, or off-chain proofs of account control. Always sign fresh nonces to avoid replay attacks and never ask users to sign raw transactions for trivial UI actions.

Common mistake
Treating a signature as proof without checking the recovered address against the claimed identity. Always compare addresses and validate nonces.

screens.title: Node Accounts vs Browser Wallet Accounts
screens.subtitle: Understanding the difference between web3.eth.getAccounts and window.ethereum

narration.text: A frequent source of confusion is the difference between accounts known to a node, such as Ganache, and accounts exposed by a user's browser wallet like MetaMask. web3. eth. getAccounts() queries the connected provider for accounts that the node manages; in a Ganache environment these are pre-funded test accounts available to your scripts. In contrast, window. ethereum and eth_requestAccounts expose the user's personal wallet accounts selected in their browser extension. For a dApp that serves users, relying on node accounts will not work: you need the user's consented wallet accounts to perform on-chain actions as that user. This is why production dApps call window. ethereum. request with method eth_requestAccounts — it prompts the wallet and returns the user-selected addresses. Another important contrast is signing: node-managed accounts can be unlocked on a local node and signed by the node; browser wallets sign internally and never give you the private key. A common mistake is mixing these models: writing UI code that assumes web3. eth. getAccounts returns the active browser account. Test this explicitly by comparing arrays returned from both calls in your dev environment. Final thought: always prefer wallet-managed signing for end-users and reserve node accounts for automated test harnesses.

keyIdea.title: Accounts comparison
keyIdea.text: web3.eth.getAccounts reads node-managed accounts; window.ethereum.eth_requestAccounts requests the user's wallet addresses and requires explicit consent.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Node vs Wallet Accounts
Node-managed accounts (Ganache)
  • Returned by web3.eth.getAccounts() when connected to a node that exposes keys.
  • Useful for automated tests and pre-funded development scripts.
  • Signing can be performed by the node if it manages unlocked accounts.
Browser wallet accounts (MetaMask)
  • Exposed via window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' }).
  • Require user consent; keys stay in the wallet and never leave the extension.
  • Recommended for production-facing dApps because of stronger user-controlled security.
Developer check
In a dev console run both web3.eth.getAccounts() and window.ethereum.request to compare outputs. If you expect user accounts, make sure you prompt eth_requestAccounts and handle the user rejecting the prompt with proper try...catch logic.

screens.title: Integrating MetaMask in a React dApp
screens.subtitle: Requesting accounts and handling user flows without touching private keys

narration.text: Integrating a browser wallet involves three clear responsibilities: request permission to access accounts, read the selected address, and delegate signing to the wallet. In React, the typical pattern creates a connect function that checks for window. ethereum, calls eth_requestAccounts inside a try... catch, and constructs a Web3 instance using window. ethereum. After successful connection you use web3. eth. getAccounts or web3Instance. eth. getAccounts to read the selected address and place it in state for your UI. Importantly, when you need to sign or send a transaction, you build the transaction payload in your dApp and then call the wallet to sign it — the wallet displays the prompt and returns a signed transaction or signature. The wallet retains the private key, so your app never sees it. A common pitfall is not handling the user rejecting the request; always detect error code 4001 and show a helpful fallback. Another pitfall is assuming window. ethereum is always present; provide a message instructing installation when absent. The following content contains the starter React connector pattern you can copy into your App. jsx and adapt to your project structure.

keyIdea.title: Wallet integration
keyIdea.text: Use eth_requestAccounts for consent, construct Web3 with window.ethereum, and let the wallet sign to keep private keys secure.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › MetaMask Integration
React connector pattern
async function connectWallet(setWeb3, setAccount, setError) {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    try {
      await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
      const web3Instance = new Web3(window.ethereum);
      setWeb3(web3Instance);
      const accounts = await web3Instance.eth.getAccounts();
      if (accounts.length > 0) {
        setAccount(accounts[0]);
      } else {
        setError('No accounts found.');
      }
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.code === 4001) setError('User rejected the connection request.');
      else setError('Error connecting: ' + err.message);
    }
  } else {
    setError('MetaMask not installed.');
  }
}
UX & errors
  • Show clear messages for 'MetaMask not installed' and 'User rejected the connection request'.
  • Do not proceed with transactions until a connected account exists.
Pro Tip
Request the minimal permissions you need and explain why you ask for them to increase user trust.

screens.title: Node.js Demo: Accounts.create, privateKeyToAccount, sign, recover
screens.subtitle: Live-coding style terminal demo with console outputs for each step

narration.text: In a terminal-style Node environment you'll run a sequence of Web3. js calls to observe account creation, import, signing, and recovery. Start by connecting Web3 to a local Ganache node. Call web3. eth. accounts. create() to generate a random account; record the address and private key locally for the test run only. Next, use privateKeyToAccount with one of Ganache's sample private keys to add an account object to web3. eth. accounts. wallet. Log the wallet to verify the account appears. Then sign a short message with the created account's private key via web3. eth. accounts. sign and print the signature. Finally, call web3. eth. accounts. recover on the message and signature and verify the recovered address matches the signer. The console outputs are your proof: a generated address, the signature string, and the recovered address. Remember: do this on a local node for learning; never paste real user keys into scripts. After running the steps, examine the logs to confirm the deterministic relation between a private key and its derived address, and reflect on how the wallet keeps keys out of the browser in production.

keyIdea.title: Terminal demo
keyIdea.text: Run create, import, sign, and recover in Node to observe address derivation and signature verification; keep keys local and disposable.

screens.title: React Starter: Connect Wallet Example Explained
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of the starter App.jsx and the expected behaviors

narration.text: The provided React starter demonstrates a minimal connect flow using window. ethereum and Web3. The component maintains state for the web3 instance, the connected account, and an error message. The connect function first checks for window. ethereum. If it exists, it asks for accounts via eth_requestAccounts which triggers the user's wallet UI. On success, a Web3 instance is created from window. ethereum and the connected account is stored in React state for UI rendering. If the user rejects the permission prompt, the error code 4001 indicates they denied access and you should display a friendly message rather than crashing. If window. ethereum is absent, instruct users to install MetaMask. The starter also shows how to conditionally render the Connect Wallet call-to-action or the connected address. For production, avoid long blocking operations on the main thread and always validate that the returned accounts array contains at least one address before trusting it. Finally, remember to handle account changes and network changes by listening to the provider events in your app for a robust UX. React Starter: Connect Wallet Example Explained means eth_requestaccounts prompts the wallet; handle rejection, absent wallets, and update ui with the connected address.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the starter app.jsx and the expected behaviors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: React connect
keyIdea.text: eth_requestAccounts prompts the wallet; handle rejection, absent wallets, and update UI with the connected address.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › React Starter Explained
Starter code core
const connectWallet = async () => {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    try {
      await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
      const web3Instance = new Web3(window.ethereum);
      setWeb3(web3Instance);
      const accounts = await web3Instance.eth.getAccounts();
      if (accounts.length > 0) setAccount(accounts[0]);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.code === 4001) setError('User rejected the connection request.');
      else setError('Error connecting: ' + err.message);
    }
  } else setError('MetaMask is not installed.');
};
Behavior expectations
  • Prompt the wallet; do not assume success.
  • Store only the connected address in state, not the private key.
  • On account change, refresh address and permissions.
Key Takeaway
This pattern delegates signing to the wallet and keeps private keys isolated from your app.

screens.title: Security Risks and Mitigations for Private Keys
screens.subtitle: Why handling keys carefully is non-negotiable and how to reduce risk

narration.text: Private keys are the single point of failure for blockchain asset control. The main risks are accidental exposure in client code, theft through XSS or malicious browser extensions, and leakage via backups or version control. To mitigate these risks, follow layered practices. First, never store private keys in client-side storage or commit them to repositories. Second, prefer wallet solutions—MetaMask, hardware wallets—so keys never leave the user device. Third, use short-lived test keys for local development and keep them segregated from production environments. Fourth, when building backend services that must hold signing keys for automated tasks, use secure HSMs or vaults that limit key export. For message signing, always employ nonces or challenges to prevent replay attacks. For UX, make clear to users what a signature request does and only ask to sign minimal necessary payloads. A common misconception is thinking encryption of a private key in client storage is sufficient; client-side environments are still vulnerable. The ultimate defense is limiting where keys exist and delegating signing to secure, audited wallet software. Security Risks and Mitigations for Private Keys means do not store private keys in client code; use wallets for user keys and secure vaults or hsms for server keys.. In practical terms, why handling keys carefully is non-negotiable and how to reduce risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security rules
keyIdea.text: Do not store private keys in client code; use wallets for user keys and secure vaults or HSMs for server keys.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Security Risks & Mitigations
Top risks
  • Exposing private keys in client code or version control.
  • Theft via cross-site scripting or malicious browser extensions.
  • Replay attacks if nonces or challenges are not used for message signing.
Mitigations
  • Delegate signing to browser wallets or hardware wallets for user keys.
  • Use HSMs or secure vaults for server-side automated keys.
  • Use ephemeral test keys locally and segregate environments.
Developer checklist
Audit where keys live, add runtime checks to prevent accidental commits, and educate users about signature prompts.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.subtitle: Practical debugging tips and safeguards when working with accounts

narration.text: Developers frequently trip over a small set of avoidable mistakes. First, importing a private key without the leading 0x will throw errors; always normalize keys before passing to privateKeyToAccount. Second, not handling the user rejecting eth_requestAccounts can break the UI. Protect against this with try... catch and explicit messages when err. code equals 4001. Third, mixing node accounts and wallet accounts leads to unexpected behavior; always choose the right source for the context: node accounts for test scripts, wallet accounts for user-driven actions. Fourth, exposing private keys in logs or committing them to a repo is a catastrophic error — add git pre-commit hooks or scanning to prevent accidental commits. Fifth, failing to use nonces for signed messages enables replay attacks; issue a server-side challenge for each login-like action. For debugging, compare addresses from create() and privateKeyToAccount() to confirm deterministic derivation, and run recover on signatures to validate correctness. Adopt these small safeguards early and they will prevent major security incidents later. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them means normalize private keys, handle user rejections, separate node vs wallet accounts, and protect repositories from leaked keys.. In practical terms, practical debugging tips and safeguards when working with accounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Normalize private keys, handle user rejections, separate node vs wallet accounts, and protect repositories from leaked keys.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Common Mistakes
Mistakes and fixes
Missing 0x
Normalize keys to include 0x before importing.
Unhandled rejection
Catch error code 4001 and show a recovery path in the UI.
Confusing account sources
Document when to use node accounts vs wallet accounts in your app.
Leaked keys
Use pre-commit hooks and secrets scanning to prevent commits of keys.
Debugging tips
  • Compare generate and recover outputs to ensure deterministic behavior.
  • Inspect provider type to confirm you're calling wallet APIs or node APIs as intended.
Key Takeaway
Small checks and clear separation of environments avoid the biggest risks when working with keys.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First: an Ethereum account is a private key and its derived public address; the private key is the secret and must be kept secure. Second: Web3. js offers methods like web3. eth. accounts. create(), privateKeyToAccount(), sign(), and recover() which are powerful for local testing and proofs of ownership, but should never be used to manage real users' private keys inside client code. Third: For production user interactions, integrate browser wallets like MetaMask via window. ethereum and eth_requestAccounts so signing happens inside the wallet and keys never leave the user's device. Fourth: Always handle error cases and user rejections gracefully and use nonces for signed messages to prevent replay attacks. Keep these points in mind when you design your dApp architecture: test locally with disposable keys, delegate user signing to trusted wallets, and apply vaults or HSMs for any server-side keys.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Separate testing from production, never expose private keys, and use wallets for user-controlled signing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
Ethereum Account
A private key and a derived public address; private key equals control.
Signing & Recover
Use sign and recover to prove ownership without exposing keys.
Browser Wallets
Integrate with MetaMask via window.ethereum and eth_requestAccounts for secure user signing.
Summary takeaway
Design systems so keys never leave secure environments. Test with disposable keys and rely on wallets for production user flows.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three one-line reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Finish with three short rules you can apply immediately. Rule one: private keys are secrets — never place them in client-side code or repositories. Rule two: for user interactions rely on browser wallets like MetaMask so signing is performed in a secure environment and only signatures are passed back to your dApp. Rule three: use Web3. js account utilities for local testing, but segregate those workflows from production systems and always use nonces when building signed-message authentication. These concise reminders help keep security top of mind while you build functionality. Before you move on, ask yourself: does my application ever need to see a user's private key? If the answer is yes, redesign the flow so the wallet or a secure vault performs the signing instead. What to Remember means keep keys secret, delegate signing to wallets, and separate test keys from production.. In practical terms, three one-line reminders to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Keep keys secret, delegate signing to wallets, and separate test keys from production.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What to Remember
Do not expose private keys
Treat keys as secrets and avoid client-side storage or commits.
Use wallets for signing
Integrate MetaMask and use eth_requestAccounts for consented access.
Segregate test keys
Use Web3.js account tools only in local test environments and never in production.
Keep these rules visible when you design features that require signing. The architecture you choose today determines how safely users' assets are protected tomorrow.
